Drone, imagery and custom detection

Your imagery, archive scenes or a new capture

The right survey starts with the right picture. If your teams already fly drones or buy satellite scenes, we run our structure, change and corridor analysis on them. If you need imagery, we source dated very-high-resolution scenes from commercial archives, or request a new capture when the archive is too old. Every report names its imagery and, where the source gives one, its capture date.

Used in: Mining · Power & utilities · Project finance & ESIA · Government & public programmes

Request a proposal Imagery and data sources

What it is

Three ways to get the right picture

Every survey depends on its imagery. A structure register needs very-high-resolution images; a cut-off record needs a known capture date; change detection needs two dated images of the same place. The first job in every proposal is to find the imagery that fits the question, at a date that matters, and to say plainly what it can and cannot show.

Start here if you fly

The imagery you already hold

Send the drone orthophotos or satellite scenes you already have, and we run the same structure, change and corridor analysis on them. Many survey and asset teams already fly their own drones; our analysis adds a reviewed register to imagery that is otherwise only looked at.

What already exists

Dated archive scenes

Dated, very-high-resolution satellite scenes of your area, sourced from commercial archives, used in your analysis and delivered as imagery. Archive coverage, dates and cloud vary by place, so we check what exists before we scope the work.

When the archive is too old

A new satellite capture

A new very-high-resolution capture of your site or corridor, requested from commercial operators. The capture date depends on satellite availability and weather, and minimum order areas apply.

How it works

How we plan the imagery

  1. Start from the question

    What the record must show, at what detail, for which date. That decides the resolution and the date window.

  2. Check what exists

    Your own imagery first, then the commercial archives, with the capture date and cloud of each candidate scene.

  3. Fill the gaps

    A new satellite capture for a time window, or a drone survey where one date or more detail matters, subject to the permits each flight requires.

  4. Name it in the report

    Every report states each image’s source and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Open data is credited as its licence requires.

Our imagery statement

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Where the date matters (cut-off dates, change detection, evidence packs) we use dated imagery: a drone survey, a purchased satellite scene or your own georeferenced imagery.

Basemaps are not survey imagery

The satellite layers behind common web maps carry no capture date. We use them to screen and plan, and Google’s, credited, to show our pipeline sample, never as delivered imagery.

What you receive

Imagery, and what it shows

  • The analysis you scoped (a structure register, change layers, a corridor survey) on the imagery named in the report
  • Archive or new scenes delivered as imagery, where scoped and where the supplier’s terms allow
  • An imagery note: each image’s source, capture date and what it can and cannot show
  • A PDF report in English or Portuguese, GIS layers in GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile, and an interactive map file that can include your survey imagery

The services behind it

Every proposal names the services it includes. These are the ones this solution draws on.

Drone and imagery

  • Analysis of your own imagerySend the drone orthophotos or satellite scenes you already have, and we run the same structure, change and corridor analysis on them.
  • Very-high-resolution satellite imagery sourcingDated, very-high-resolution satellite scenes of your area sourced from commercial archives, used in your analysis and delivered as imagery.
  • New satellite capture of your siteA new very-high-resolution satellite capture of your site or corridor, requested from commercial operators for when archive imagery is too old. The capture date depends on satellite availability and weather.

Limits

What imagery can and cannot do

What it gives you

  • The best available picture for the question and the date
  • Analysis on the imagery your teams already hold
  • A named source and capture date for every image

Its limits

  • No guaranteed capture date or revisit
  • Optical satellite and drone imagery cannot see the ground under cloud
  • Nothing smaller than the imagery’s resolution can be mapped
  • Archives do not cover every place and period

Frequently asked questions

What imagery can you work with?

Georeferenced drone orthophotos and satellite scenes, typically as GeoTIFF. Automatic structure detection needs very-high-resolution imagery; coarser imagery supports larger patterns such as land-cover change. We check a sample before scoping the work, and results depend on the imagery’s quality and resolution.

Will a new satellite capture arrive on a set date?

No. A new capture is requested for a time window, and the date depends on satellite availability and weather, especially in the rainy season. Where one date matters, a drone survey, subject to the permits the flight requires, or the nearest dated archive scene is usually the better plan.

Which satellites do you use?

We choose per job from commercial archives and operators, based on the date you need, the season, cloud and the resolution the job needs, and name the source and capture date in the report.

Do you deliver the satellite view from web maps?

No. Map-service basemaps carry no capture date and their terms do not make them survey imagery. We use them to screen and plan, and Google’s, credited, to show our pipeline sample on this site, never as delivered imagery or as the basis of a dated record.

Is there a minimum area for archive or new imagery?

Yes. Commercial suppliers set minimum order areas for archive scenes and new captures, which we take into account when we plan the imagery for your route or site and set out in the proposal.

Tell us what imagery you have, and what you need it to show.

A sample orthophoto or scene, the area, and the dates that matter. We check what exists and reply with an imagery plan and a written proposal.
